subject: physics
title: Position
summary: Position describes where an object is in space relative to a reference point — like a dog 5 meters to the right of a tree, or a rocket at (3, 2) on a grid. Explore how choosing a different reference point or a different direction changes what "here" means, and how position is the starting block for describing all motion.

crossReferences.note: Displacement is simply the change in position — a single straight-line vector from the starting position to the ending position.

compareCandidate.label: Position vs. distance
compareCandidate.description: Position is a location — "the dog is 4 m LEFT of the gate" — while distance is length moved. Position always needs a reference point and a direction; distance is just a size with no direction at all.

plainLanguageExplanation: Position just answers the question "where is it?" — but there's a catch: you can only answer it compared to something else. "My house is at 24" by itself is meaningless; "my house is 24 steps from the fountain, to the east" is a real answer. The thing you measure from is the reference point. In this model you'll place a child on a long line and read off where it sits: how many steps to the right of the mailbox, or 3 squares over and 2 squares up on a grid. Move the reference point and the same child gets a new number — but it hasn't actually moved — which shows that position is always measured relative to something. Position is the single most important place to start in mechanics, because everything else (distance, displacement, speed, velocity) is just a fancier way of talking about how position changes.

keyFacts.label: Definition
keyFacts.value: Where an object is located, measured relative to a chosen reference point

keyFacts.label: Reference point
keyFacts.value: The fixed spot you measure from — if it changes, the position numbers change too

keyFacts.label: Always relative
keyFacts.value: A position statement needs a direction and a distance ("5 m left of the flag"), not just a number

keyFacts.label: Coordinates
keyFacts.value: On a grid, position is a pair like (3, 2) — one number for each axis

keyFacts.label: Sign tells side
keyFacts.value: A negative number (+x or -x) usually means a position on the opposite side of the reference point

keyFacts.label: Foundation for motion
keyFacts.value: Change in position over time is how we define speed and velocity later

whyItMatters: Position is the very idea the ball starts from 0. GPS gives your position, a map shows a city's position, and a sport score tells position in a race. In physics, nearly everything else in mechanics is a measure of how position changes — if you cannot describe position clearly, you cannot describe motion. Understanding reference points also explains real-world arguments like "the train seems still but the platform is racing" — it depends on what you chose as the reference point.
tagline: Where is it? Compared to what?
didYouKnow: The word 'position' shares its root with 'place' and 'put' — it's literally about where something is put. GPS satellites work the same way: your position is read off by measuring how far you are (in signals) from several reference satellites.
conditions: Locations on a map or grid
compareReason: Position is a point measured from something; distance is an amount of movement. Seeing both on the same number line is the fastest way to untangle them.
